content:
Earlier this year, I swapped a gasoline-powered mower for a robotic mower that can be controlled with an iPhone. Users can manually drive the robot along the edges of the lawn to build a virtual map. Once set up, the robot will automatically mow according to a preset schedule.

Recently, I tested another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after a few weeks of testing, I think this machine may be easier to use for many people.

Camera-Assisted Automatic Mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year lies in how each understands your lawn.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower along the boundary with my iPhone in order to create the initial map.

On the other hand, the TerraMow V1000 uses a system the manufacturer calls TerraVision 2.0. Equipped with three cameras, the mower can automatically map out the lawn area, without the need to lay boundary wires in the ground or install an additional RTK antenna.

The automatic initial mapping process takes longer, but I think it may be simpler for people who are less familiar with computer technology.

To verify this, I asked my mother, who lives in another state, to set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own, without me assisting her on the side. She said everything worked fine. That said, I'm not entirely sure she would have the patience to first manually drive the robot along the entire boundary with her phone and mark out all the areas to avoid.

In my front yard, there were a few small issues during the automatic mapping process. There is no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbour's, so the TerraMow initially included part of my neighbour's lawn in my map.

I set that area as a no-go zone in the app, and the problem was resolved. That said, if there is no clearly visible boundary between two lawns, extra care is needed when creating the initial map.

Peeking Through the Mower's Cameras

The cameras on the TerraMow also enable one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can display a live feed of what the mower sees while it is working.

During testing, I used the screen mirroring feature on my iPhone to project this footage on a large display onto my Mac. I could sit indoors working while watching from the mower's perspective as it moved around the backyard.

This feature is not essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more interesting, and sometimes it can explain why the mower slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 does not have a corresponding camera feed feature.

Beyond that, the two iPhone apps have a lot in common. Both support preset schedules, mowing mode adjustments, zone划分, no-go zone marking, and remote control of the mower.

TerraMow has an especially thoughtful design for that last feature. In addition to the traditional left and right virtual control sticks, its app also offers a single-hand joystick mode. You can hold the iPhone normally and use your thumb to control the mower's direction.

Manually driving the mower with an iPhone is not the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run automatically according to a preset schedule without human intervention. That said, TerraMow's joystick mode is quite fun for tidying up the small patches the robot may have missed.

Sometimes I almost feel like I'm controlling the robot with telekinesis (the fun kind). I hold the iPhone and walk alongside the mower, and with a gentle nudge of my thumb, the robot moves in the direction I control it.

Every robotic mower app should copy this design.

A More Aggressive Mower

The TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut closer to the ground and was also louder when running.

I wouldn't say the TerraMow is 'noisy,' but the difference is noticeable. The Anthbot is very quiet when running—quiet enough that even if it's out mowing at night with its headlights on, you'd almost forget it's still running.

Because TerraMow relies on camera navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. So scheduling daytime mowing becomes more important.

The V1000 itself feels solid, and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage to cover the charging base, whereas Anthbot's garage has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow has been consistently reliable. I relied on it to mow daily for several weeks in a row, and the entire time there was no need for any human intervention.

When Adaptive Mapping Is Too 'Clever'

The same kind of visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower continuously adjusts the map based on what it sees. After each session, saving these changes takes quite a long time, during which you can't do anything else in the app.

After several days of heavy rain, I ran into an interesting edge case. A puddle of water had collected in one spot in the yard, and the TerraMow cleverly avoided that area during its next run.

Inside the circular area that was skipped, the weeds grew taller and taller. After some time, the mower seemed to mistake the weeds there for something that needed to be continuously avoided, and even after the ground dried out, that area continued to be skipped.

I used the remote control function in the app to manually drive the mower over and cut down the taller grass there, and the problem was resolved. After that area returned to normal, automatic mowing also resumed there.

Regular edging also helps the TerraMow approach boundaries more confidently. Tall grass growing along unclear lines may otherwise be mistaken for an obstacle rather than part of the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more on user-defined boundaries and obstacles. That method requires more preparatory work, but it can avoid the situation where the map 'goes back on its word' about the same patch of grass.

9to5Mac Conclusion

After using both systems, for most people I lean toward recommending TerraMow's camera-based approach.

For me, burying wires in the ground is completely impractical, and installing an RTK base station means placing, powering, and maintaining extra hardware. TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation is not flawless. Initial mapping takes longer, ambiguous boundaries require manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook an overgrown patch of weeds for a permanent obstacle.

All of these issues are manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers easier setup, reliable automatic mowing, a captivating live camera feed, and the best manual control experience of any robotic mower app I've used.

I genuinely enjoy taking care of the garden, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing this chore over to a robot frees up time to tend to flower beds, do edging, and handle detail work, while keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 excels in this regard, and I would recommend it, especially for users who want a robotic mower but don't want to lay wires in the ground, install an RTK antenna, or walk the entire yard holding their phone from start to finish.

Amazon currently prices the TerraMow V1000 at $999, available after using a $200 coupon code on the deals site. The product is also available on the TerraMow official website.
